# When does three-dimensional elastic contact with Coulomb friction admit a quasistatic solution?

Mechanics tabs: Contact

Scientific status Open

Problem type Existence and quasistatic evolution

Literature audit 30 September 2026

Statement v1.0

Short reading layer · the question

A basic friction law becomes a difficult continuum problem when contact pressure, contact region, stick–slip state, and elastic deformation must all be determined together.

A deformable elastic solid pressed against an obstacle must decide, point by point, whether it is separated, sticking, or sliding.

The normal contact pressure is unknown. But Coulomb’s friction limit is proportional to that same unknown pressure:

$$
|\mathbf t_t|\le -f\,t_n.
$$

Thus the normal and tangential contact problems are intrinsically coupled.

Classical mathematics proves existence in important restricted settings, including three-dimensional problems with sufficiently small friction. Recent work has now obtained sharp results for the general two-dimensional problem.

The corresponding sharp three-dimensional theory remains incomplete.

## Why it matters

Dry friction is among the simplest and oldest constitutive laws in mechanics. Elasticity is equally fundamental.

Their coupling controls:

  * brakes and friction-induced vibration;
  * bolted and mechanical joints;
  * press fits and seals;
  * tires and sliding interfaces;
  * forming processes;
  * particulate contacts;
  * robotic grasping and manipulation.

Yet the continuum problem is mathematically subtle because the state of the interface is itself unknown.

At each contact point one must determine simultaneously:

$$
\boxed{
\text{contact or separation}
\quad+\quad
\text{normal pressure}
\quad+\quad
\text{stick or slip}
\quad+\quad
\text{friction traction}.
}
$$

The problem is therefore a canonical example of how elementary local mechanical laws can produce a difficult global continuum theory.

Conditional regularity criteria (Beale-Kato-Majda via vorticity, originally formulated for Euler and adapted to Navier-Stokes, and the Prodi-Serrin-Ladyzhenskaya scale-critical integrability conditions) convert control of a single critical quantity into full smoothness.

## The state of solutions in 2026

Where things stand today:

  * Exact solutions: a settled catalog for symmetric flows, still growing slowly at the margins
  * Numerical solutions: mature and spectacularly accurate for engineering, with reliability that degrades as turbulence modeling carries more of the load
  * For unforced 3D Navier–Stokes, neither global regularity for arbitrary admissible smooth data nor a smooth-data blowup example is established. The announced forced C/D construction does not answer that remaining question.

Exact solutions, numerical approximations and the unforced global-regularity question are different meanings of solving Navier–Stokes. The September 2026 announcement concerns forced breakdown. See also: progress page

The strongest unconditional 3D result remains Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg partial regularity: for suitable weak solutions, the singular set has one-dimensional parabolic Hausdorff measure zero. Conditional regularity criteria (Beale-Kato-Majda via vorticity, originally formulated for Euler and adapted to Navier-Stokes, and the Prodi-Serrin-Ladyzhenskaya scale-critical integrability conditions) convert control of a single critical quantity into full smoothness.

Active directions include convex integration and the structure of non-uniqueness below the Leray-Hopf class, quantitative regularity and blowup-rate results, computer-assisted analysis of candidate self-similar blowup scenarios, and stochastic regularization questions. The scaling gap (the known a priori estimates are supercritical relative to the natural scaling of the equations) is still the central obstruction, and it's why incremental improvements haven't closed the problem.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A solution is provided to the Bruxelles Problem, a geometric decision problem originally posed in 1825, that asks for a synthetic construction to determine when ten points in 3-space lie on a quadric surface, a surface given by the vanishing of a degree-2 polynomial. The solution constructs four new points that are coplanar precisely when the ten original points lie on a quadric surface. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
